newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portuguese inflation to ease despite May result.
newsitem.headline: Portuguese inflation to ease despite May result.

text.p: Portugal's inflation was higher than expected in May, but analysts expect price pressures to ease during the rest of the year and see government achieving its 1997 inflation target of 2.5 percent.
Portugal's month-on-month inflation stood at 0.7 percent in May, giving a year-on-year increase of 2.1 percent.
The main cause of the jump was attributed to food, notably potato and pork, and drink prices which rose 1.1 percent against just 0.2 percent in April and 0.5 percent in May last year.
The rise was higher than analysts' forecasts which had been for a year-on-year rise of between 1.4 and 1.8 percent in May.

Analysts said that even though the average inflation rate might have to be revised slightly higher this year after the May result, the overall fall in inflation would only be interrupted if there were an abnormal trend in the food and drink segment.

"This (May) inflation result breaks the trend of excellent numbers that we have seen, but in terms of the average annual rate, it will not change our estimate for the end of the year by very much," said Nuno Godinho of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Pedro Braz Teixeira of Banco Santander de Negocios Portugal (BSNP) said: "The results are due to very specific factors (potato and pork prices) and do not spoil the downward trend that we have seen recently."
He said he was revising upwards his estimate for average annual inflation by 0.1 to 0.2 percentage points to nearly 2.5 percent.

Martim Amaral Neto of Banco ESSI said: "Even though the May inflation figure was a shock, the average annual rate should stay below 2.5 percent and enable Portugal to meet the Maastricht convergence goal."
Most analysts said a question mark still hung over the behaviour of food and drink prices during the remainder of 1997.

"Most of the components of the prices index are evolving well, but I think that food prices could continue to push the consumer prices index higher in the coming months," said Giovanni Polastri of 4Cast in London.
However, Martim Amaral Neto said: "I think most of the impact from the surge in potato and pork prices will be diluted in the coming months."
